nary_nodes.label: Munich court rules Suno AI violated copyrights
evidence: The Munich Regional Court ruled on Friday that Suno AI, a US-based company, which generates songs from text prompts. has violated copyrights and has to disclose illicit revenues.

nary_nodes.label: GEMA initiated lawsuit against Suno AI
evidence: The lawsuit initiated in January 2025 by GEMA, Germany's state-mandated licensing agency, argued that Suno trained its AI models on copyrighted music without obtaining licences or compensating its rights holders.

nary_nodes.label: Suno AI must pay damages
evidence: According to the verdict, Suno will have to pay damages that have yet to be quantified.

nary_nodes.label: Suno AI disagrees with court ruling
evidence: Suno has disagreed with the ruling and said it would evaluate all available options, including an appeal.

nary_nodes.label: Suno AI considers appeal
evidence: Suno has disagreed with the ruling and said it would evaluate all available options, including an appeal.

nary_nodes.label: Verdict has global significance
evidence: "This is a verdict of global significance," Gema CEO Tobias Holzmueller told Reuters.

nary_nodes.label: Lawsuit tests copyright law application to AI music
evidence: The lawsuit has been closely watched, as it is one of the first major cases anywhere in the world to test how traditional copyright law applies to AI music training and AI-generated music outputs.

nary_nodes.label: German court lacks jurisdiction over US AI training
evidence: Among Suno's arguments was the fact that the German court does not have proper jurisdiction to rule on AI model training activities that occurred exclusively inside the United States.

nary_nodes.label: Proceedings could determine AI music licensing and infringement
evidence: The proceedings could help determine whether AI music companies must obtain licenses before training their models on copyrighted songs, and whether AI-generated music that closely resembles existing songs constitutes copyright infringement.

nary_nodes.label: GEMA's goal is licensing negotiations with Suno
evidence: "Our goal is not to clear Suno from the face of the earth, but obviously to get into licensing negotiations on an eye-to-eye level, which was not possible with Suno so far," explains GEMA CEO Tobias Holzmüller

nary_nodes.label: Suno AI is largest and most successful AI music model company
evidence: who describes the company as "by far the largest and commercially most successful of all AI music models."

nary_nodes.label: Suno AI pursues aggressive business strategy
evidence: He believes Suno pursues a much more aggressive business strategy than its competitors.

nary_nodes.label: Case outcome linked to creator compensation for AI training
evidence: The outcome of this case is also linked to another central question: How should creators be compensated when their music is used to train generative AI systems?

nary_nodes.label: GEMA won related case against OpenAI
evidence: Last year, GEMA won a related case against OpenAI before the same court.

nary_nodes.label: OpenAI unlawfully trained on copyrighted song lyrics
evidence: It found that OpenAI unlawfully trained its AI models on copyrighted song lyrics and reproduced them via ChatGPT without authorization.

nary_nodes.label: OpenAI ordered to cease, disclose, pay damages
evidence: OpenAI was ordered to cease and desist from reproducing the works in the model, to disclose information and pay damages.

nary_nodes.label: OpenAI pursues appeal
evidence: But as the company pursues an appeal, the ruling remains non-final.

nary_nodes.label: OpenAI ruling remains non-final
evidence: But as the company pursues an appeal, the ruling remains non-final.

nary_nodes.label: Current lawsuit focuses on entire music pieces
evidence: In contrast to that decision, the current lawsuit does not focus on song lyrics, but on entire music pieces.

nary_nodes.label: Lawsuit important due to music collecting society initiator
evidence: One of the aspects that makes this lawsuit important is that it has not been initiated by a private company or record label, but rather by a music collecting society, notes Martin Senftleben, professor of intellectual property law at the Amsterdam Law School.

nary_nodes.label: Music collecting society initiatives are inclusive
evidence: Such initiatives "are particularly important because, by definition, you could say that they're more inclusive," Senftleben tells DW.

nary_nodes.label: GEMA membership is inclusive
evidence: "You can become a GEMA member even if you're not a very well-known high-profile artist or composer.

nary_nodes.label: Remuneration for AI users can reach broader rights holders
evidence: And that means there's a chance of bringing remuneration for AI users to a much broader group of rights holders."

nary_nodes.label: GEMA claims Suno trained AI without permission or payment
evidence: GEMA claims that Suno trained its AI on copyrighted music without permission or payment to songwriters, composers and publishers represented by the German music collecting society.

nary_nodes.label: GEMA claims Suno benefits commercially without compensating artists
evidence: GEMA also says that the US-based company is commercially benefiting from those works without compensating the artists.

nary_nodes.label: GEMA demonstrated AI songs similar to originals
evidence: During the court proceedings, GEMA demonstrated this by prompting Suno AI to create tracks with the original lyrics of different popular songs in its repertoire, including "Forever Young" by Alphaville, "Mambo No. 5" by Lou Bega, "Daddy Cool" by Boney M., "Cheri Cheri Lady" by Modern Talking and "Atemlos durch die Nacht," written by Kristina Bach and popularized by Helene Fischer.

nary_nodes.label: Suno admits original songs used for AI training
evidence: Suno admits that the original songs at the center of GEMA's lawsuit are among the numerous pieces that were used to train the AI model.

nary_nodes.label: AI companies claim fair use/TDM exception for data ingestion
evidence: AI companies such as Suno claim that the ingestion of data for AI training can be done freely on the basis of what is known as "fair use" in the US and the "text and data mining exception" rule in the EU.

nary_nodes.label: Licence-free AI training under copyright law is contested
evidence: But whether such licence-free AI training is allowed under copyright law remains heavily contested globally.

nary_nodes.label: Courts examine if AI uses harm economic market of creators
evidence: In different lawsuits around the world, courts are now examining whether such uses harm the economic market of the original creators through unfair competition.

nary_nodes.label: Lawsuit novelty is GEMA's focus on AI output
evidence: "The novelty in the lawsuit is that GEMA does not focus on the AI training stage," explains Senftleben.

nary_nodes.label: GEMA bridges gap between AI training use and market harm at output level
evidence: By basing their claim on tests that demonstrate that these AI systems generate songs that have similarities with copyright-protected works from their repertoire, "they bridge this gap between relevant use now taking place in AI training, and the market harm done at AI output level," he adds.

nary_nodes.label: AI industry claims AI models learn like humans
evidence: Similarly, the AI industry claims this analogy applies to how their models are trained — by absorbing countless creative works in order to generate new ones.

nary_nodes.label: Rights holders view AI models as copying and exploiting works
evidence: But from the rights holders' perspective, AI models are rather copying and commercially exploiting their works.

nary_nodes.label: Argument that AI learns like humans is ridiculous
evidence: This argument that an AI learns from music and is inspired by it like a human being is "completely ridiculous," notes Tobias Holzmüller.

nary_nodes.label: AI processing of sound files incomparable to human brain
evidence: These are concepts that come from the human brain and have been designed for the human brain, and not for a machine that is able to digest millions of sound files in split seconds.

I mean, just the amount of sheer data — they say it's data; for us, it's music — that these machines have swallowed up and then digested and are now spitting out, this is completely incomparable to what's happening in a human brain.

nary_nodes.label: Humanizing AI machines is not logical or moral
evidence: "To humanize these machines by using these concepts is not logical — and it's certainly not moral."

nary_nodes.label: Suno users generate 7 million songs daily
evidence: Across Suno's platform globally, users collectively generate roughly 7 million songs per day.
Around 75,000 of them end up on streaming services daily, adds Holzmüller.

nary_nodes.label: High volume of AI music generation is toxic for music ecosystem
evidence: "This is definitely where it's not sustainable anymore, but really toxic for the music ecosystem."

nary_nodes.label: Price tag on AI output needed for sustainable music model
evidence: "If you want to create a sustainable model where you accept that AI music is here to stay, but at the same time, that it shouldn't push human-created music out of the market, the only way to tackle this is to put a price tag on the output," says the CEO of GEMA.

nary_nodes.label: Free AI sounds will outcompete human music
evidence: "Because otherwise you will have free-of-charge AI sounds that will outcompete human music in a lot of circumstances."

nary_nodes.label: Increased AI sound costs via licenses could level playing field
evidence: For Holzmüller, if licences lead to an increase in costs in AI-created sounds to a point that they are as expensive as human-created songs, it could provide a level playing field.

nary_nodes.label: People will continue to use human music if costs are equal
evidence: "Then — it's my firm belief — people will continue to use human music, because it has this additional element."
